case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may extend a Bivens damages remedy to an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officials—at least in the rare circumstance where officials commit egregious abuse and then deliberately block the inmate from using the executive branch’s grievance/remedial processes.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Amendment VIII (Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause), as enforced through an implied damages action under Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics (1971).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (federal prison officials) argue the Fourth Circuit improperly created a new Bivens cause of action for prisoner excessive-force claims, contrary to the Supreme Court’s modern Bivens framework (especially Ziglar v. Abbasi, Hernandez v. Mesa, and Egbert v. Boule), which treats Bivens expansion as a 'disfavored' judicial activity. They contend the existence of alternative remedial structures in the prison context (e.g., the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and other executive/legislative tools) and the separation-of-powers concerns surrounding prison administration are 'special factors' that require courts to leave any damages remedy to Congress, not the judiciary. The United States as amicus supports this view, emphasizing institutional costs such as chilling frontline prison decisionmaking and disruption to prison operations, and urging the Court to reverse or at least prevent further expansion of Bivens into excessive-force claims.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Fields) argues the Fourth Circuit did not open the door to routine excessive-force Bivens suits; it recognized only a narrow extension for a 'rare case' involving 'rogue' officers committing 'egregious physical abuse with no imaginable penological benefit' and then intentionally withholding or thwarting the very administrative remedies the executive branch provides to address misconduct. On this view, the usual rationale against Bivens expansion (the availability of alternative remedies) collapses when officers themselves deliberately make those alternatives unavailable, and recognizing a damages remedy in that extraordinary setting is consistent with (rather than contrary to) the Court’s two-step Bivens inquiry. Respondent also characterizes petitioners’ objections as attacking an overbroad version of the Fourth Circuit’s holding that the court did not actually adopt.
key_precedents: Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)
Booker v. S.C. Dep’t of Corr., 855 F.3d 533 (4th Cir. 2017)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s best point is that intentional obstruction can make the BOP grievance process functionally unavailable, risking an accountability vacuum; if Egbert turned on case-by-case “adequacy,” that would be powerful. But Egbert’s instruction is structural: once Congress or the Executive has supplied an alternative remedial framework, courts may not extend Bivens based on allegations that the framework was thwarted in a particular case, because that invites precisely the “rare-case” line-drawing Abbasi and Egbert reject. Carlson does not control because this excessive-force claim against line officers presents a meaningfully different context and implicates prison administration in a way that supplies at least one rational reason to hesitate—especially given Congress’s PLRA choices. I would therefore vote to reverse on narrow grounds: new context plus special factors (alternative structures and separation-of-powers concerns) foreclose extending Bivens here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: that officers’ alleged obstruction of the BOP grievance process makes the “alternative remedial structure” illusory and creates a remedial void. But under Egbert v. Boule the question is not whether the alternative works perfectly in a particular case; it is whether Congress or the Executive has provided a remedial framework such that a court has reason to hesitate before implying a new damages action—especially in prison administration, where separation-of-powers concerns are at their apex. Even assuming Carlson is the closest analogue, an excessive-force claim against line officers is still a new context, and crafting a “rare-case” carveout when officials thwart remedies is precisely the kind of policy-line drawing that Abbasi and Egbert forbid courts to undertake. The Eighth Amendment’s text does not itself create a cause of action for damages against federal officers, and any additional remedy for obstruction or abuse in federal prisons is for Congress to authorize.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: that officers’ alleged obstruction of the BOP grievance process makes the “alternative remedial structure” illusory and risks a remedial vacuum. But Egbert makes the relevant inquiry institutional, not case-specific; the existence of an administratively created remedial framework (and other tools like discipline, transfer, and injunctive relief) is itself a rational reason to leave any additional damages remedy to Congress, even if it is allegedly frustrated in a particular instance. Moreover, treating obstruction as the trigger for a new Bivens action invites precisely the line-drawing and case-by-case expansion that Abbasi and Egbert sought to foreclose, while pulling courts into prison-administration disputes with substantial separation-of-powers costs. As Justice Roberts notes, Congress’s regulation of prisoner litigation through the PLRA without authorizing personal-capacity damages in this setting reinforces that it is not for us to create an implied remedy here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to emphasize Egbert’s structural caution and its skepticism toward case-by-case assessments of an alternative scheme’s “adequacy.” But their framing still presupposes a remedial structure that is meaningfully available; on these pleadings, the officers’ alleged deliberate obstruction is not “imperfection” but functional nullification of the only channel the government invokes, creating an accountability vacuum for egregious Eighth Amendment force. Carlson remains the closest analogue in the core federal-prison abuse setting, and cabining relief to situations where (1) line officers commit purposeless, excessive force and (2) intentionally foreclose the ARP does not entail broad prison management so much as preventing officers from insulating unconstitutional conduct from any remedy. Justice Thomas’s separation-of-powers concern cuts both ways here: abstention in this narrow sabotage scenario effectively licenses Executive officials to defeat Congress’s chosen administrative process and leave constitutional rights practically unenforced.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that deliberate obstruction can make the ARP functionally unavailable, and as a practical matter that is deeply troubling. But Egbert—just as the Chief Justice emphasizes—treats the “alternative remedial structure” inquiry as structural and categorical: once Congress/the Executive has created a remedial framework, we do not engage in case-by-case assessments of its adequacy or whether officials frustrated it in a particular instance, because that very tailoring is the policy work Abbasi says courts are not equipped to do. A “rare-case” carveout keyed to obstruction plus egregious force is still line-drawing about when an implied damages action should exist, and that is precisely the kind of incremental expansion Egbert was written to foreclose, especially in prison administration. The better course is to enforce existing mechanisms (including equitable relief and non-Bivens accountability routes) and leave any new personal-capacity damages remedy to Congress in the PLRA era.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson offer the strongest pushback: that officers’ alleged obstruction of the BOP grievance process renders Egbert’s “alternative remedial structure” rationale inapplicable and leaves an intolerable remedial gap. But Egbert does not make the availability or adequacy of an administrative remedy case-specific; it asks whether Congress or the Executive has created a remedial scheme such that courts have reason to hesitate before implying a new damages action, and alleged frustration of that scheme in a particular case is itself a reason to leave the solution to Congress (e.g., criminal sanctions, discipline, or statutory damages), not to expand Article III power. This claim also remains a “new context” relative to Carlson, as the mechanism of injury (episodic force by line officers) and the policy implications for prison discipline and operations differ in ways Abbasi treats as meaningful. As Justice Kagan notes, creating a “rare-case” carveout would invite line-drawing and incremental expansion inconsistent with our separation-of-powers precedents, so I would reverse.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best equitable point: if officers deliberately thwart the BOP Administrative Remedy Program, the government’s cited “alternative remedial structure” can be functionally unavailable, risking an accountability gap. But Egbert frames the inquiry institutionally, not plaintiff-specifically, and it rejects using alleged inadequacy or frustration of an existing scheme as the trigger for a new implied damages action; obstruction allegations show a need for better enforcement or statutory supplementation, not judicial creation of a new cause of action. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, this remains a new context meaningfully different from Carlson, and the Fourth Circuit’s “rare-case” carveout would require line-drawing and incremental expansion that Abbasi/Egbert sought to foreclose. On an institutionalist approach grounded in precedent and separation of powers, the proper course is to reverse and leave any additional damages remedy for federal prisoners to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s best point is that deliberate obstruction of the BOP Administrative Remedy Program can make the government’s cited “alternative remedial structure” illusory in practice, risking an accountability gap for egregious force. But Egbert’s inquiry is structural and separation-of-powers-based: as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, once Congress or the Executive has provided a remedial framework, courts are not to conduct case-by-case adequacy/availability assessments to justify implying a new damages action. Moreover, treating obstruction as the trigger for a “rare-case” Bivens extension would require judicial line-drawing about degrees of obstruction and egregiousness—precisely the incremental expansion Abbasi and Egbert reject. Carlson remains a different context (medical indifference causing death), and the differences in conduct and prison-administration implications supply at least one rational reason to pause, which ends the analysis under Egbert.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to stress Egbert’s structural language and its skepticism of case-by-case “adequacy” inquiries, but their framing assumes the existence of a genuinely available alternative in the first place. Where, as pled, officers intentionally thwart the ARP to prevent any review, the Court is not “second-guessing” the sufficiency of Congress’s remedial calibration; it is confronting executive nullification of the very channel Egbert treats as a reason for judicial restraint, producing a remedial vacuum for serious Eighth Amendment abuse. Justice Thomas’s separation-of-powers concern cuts both ways: abstention here risks insulating unconstitutional force precisely because the executive can disable oversight mechanisms at will, and a narrow rule tied to deliberate obstruction plus gratuitous force remains administrable without inviting generalized prison management. Carlson’s core accountability logic for federal prison mistreatment remains the closest analogue, and nothing in Abbasi/Egbert compels treating this obstruction-triggered vacuum as a reason to deny any damages remedy.

John Roberts.reasoning: This Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officials arises in a new Bivens context beyond the three settings the Court has recognized (Bivens, Davis, and Carlson), and under Ziglar v. Abbasi we may not extend Bivens where "special factors" counsel hesitation. Egbert v. Boule instructs that if there is any rational reason to think Congress is better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy—particularly in sensitive areas like prison administration and federalism-adjacent separation-of-powers concerns—courts must refrain. The availability of the Bureau of Prisons Administrative Remedy Program, the PLRA’s remedial and screening framework, and other executive/legislative tools constitutes an “alternative remedial structure,” and Egbert makes clear that alleged inadequacy or even obstruction of such processes does not authorize courts to create a new implied damages action. A narrow holding reversing the Fourth Circuit preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to this Court’s recent precedents limiting Bivens expansions and leaving any additional remedy to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment’s text prohibits cruel and unusual punishments, but it does not itself authorize an implied damages action against federal officers; creating such a remedy is a legislative task, not a judicial one. This case concededly arises in a new Bivens context (an excessive-force claim in the federal prison setting), and under Egbert v. Boule a court may not extend Bivens if there is even one rational reason to think Congress is better suited to decide whether to create a damages remedy. The existence of alternative remedial structures in the prison context (including the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and other executive/legislative tools), along with separation-of-powers and prison-administration concerns, are “special factors” requiring hesitation under Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert. Even if officers allegedly thwarted administrative remedies in a particular case, that counsels reliance on Congress to craft an appropriate response rather than judicial expansion of Bivens beyond the three recognized contexts (Bivens, Davis, and Carlson).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: This case arises in a new Bivens context because the Court has never recognized an implied damages action for an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officials, and it meaningfully differs from Carlson v. Green’s medical-indifference setting. Under Egbert v. Boule and Ziglar v. Abbasi, courts may not extend Bivens if there is even a single rational reason to think Congress is better positioned to decide whether to create a damages remedy, and prison administration and officer decisionmaking present acute separation-of-powers and institutional-cost concerns. The existence of alternative remedial structures—such as the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and other executive/legislative tools—forecloses extension under Egbert even if those processes are alleged to be inadequate or obstructed in a particular case. Whatever the appeal of remedying egregious misconduct, the Constitution’s Amendment VIII does not itself authorize damages, and the decision to add that remedy in the federal-prison context belongs to Congress, not the judiciary.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Carlson v. Green recognized a Bivens damages remedy under the Eighth Amendment for serious mistreatment of federal prisoners, and an egregious, purposeless excessive-force claim is closely analogous to that core prison-abuse context. Under Abbasi and Hernandez, courts hesitate to extend Bivens where Congress or the Executive has provided alternative remedial structures, but Egbert’s “alternative remedies” rationale weakens where, as alleged here, officers themselves deliberately render the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program functionally unavailable by obstructing grievances—leaving no meaningful avenue for accountability. In that rare circumstance, denying any damages remedy would create an intolerable gap in enforcement of the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause and would predictably fall hardest on the most vulnerable people in federal custody. Limiting relief to this narrow category also respects separation-of-powers concerns by avoiding a broad, systemic reworking of prison administration while still providing a remedy for unconstitutional abuse deliberately insulated from internal review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Fields’s claim arises in a new Bivens context: unlike Carlson v. Green (medical indifference leading to death), this is an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against line prison officers, and Ziglar v. Abbasi instructs courts to treat such extensions as "disfavored" and to ask whether any special factors counsel hesitation. Under Egbert v. Boule, the existence of any alternative remedial structure—here the BOP Administrative Remedy Program, other internal discipline mechanisms, and potential FTCA avenues—generally forecloses recognizing a new implied damages action even if those alternatives are imperfect or allegedly frustrated in a given case. The separation-of-powers concerns are acute in prison administration, and Congress’s regulation of prisoner litigation through the PLRA without creating a personal-capacity damages remedy reinforces that the judiciary should not supply one. However egregious the alleged abuse, Abbasi and Egbert make the availability and design of remedies a legislative/executive choice, so the Fourth Circuit’s narrow carve-out still amounts to an impermissible Bivens expansion.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: This case arises in a new Bivens context because an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officials is meaningfully different from Carlson v. Green’s Eighth Amendment medical-indifference claim, and thus triggers the modern two-step framework. Under Egbert v. Boule, if there is even a single rational reason to think Congress is better positioned to authorize a damages remedy, courts must refrain; prison administration and officer discipline present separation-of-powers and institutional-competence concerns that readily supply such reasons. The existence of alternative remedial structures—such as the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and other executive/legislative mechanisms—counsels hesitation even if they do not provide complete relief, and alleged obstruction of those processes does not expand Article III courts’ authority to create new causes of action. Any further damages remedy for federal prisoners is a policy choice for Congress, not an implied judicial remedy under Bivens.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: This case arises in a new Bivens context because the Court has recognized implied damages remedies in only three settings (Bivens, Davis, and Carlson), and an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officials is meaningfully different from Carlson’s medical-indifference context. Under Egbert v. Boule and Ziglar v. Abbasi, if there is even one rational reason to think Congress is better positioned to decide whether to create a damages remedy, courts must not extend Bivens; prison administration and officer decisionmaking present acute separation-of-powers and workability concerns. The Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and other executive/legislative mechanisms constitute alternative remedial structures that, even if imperfect or allegedly obstructed in a particular case, counsel hesitation under Egbert’s framework. Recognizing a “rare-case” carveout would invite line-drawing and expansion inconsistent with the Court’s repeated admonition that extending Bivens is a disfavored judicial activity.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Egbert v. Boule, extending Bivens is a “disfavored” judicial activity and a court must not recognize a new implied damages action if there is even a single reason to pause, including the existence of an alternative remedial structure authorized by Congress or the Executive. This Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim arises in a new context beyond the Court’s recognized Bivens settings (Bivens, Davis, and Carlson), and prison administration presents separation-of-powers concerns that Ziglar v. Abbasi identifies as a paradigmatic “special factor” counseling hesitation. The Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and the availability of injunctive relief constitute alternative mechanisms that, under Egbert and Schweiker v. Chilicky, can foreclose a Bivens extension even if they do not provide money damages or complete relief. Whatever the appeal of a narrow remedy for egregious misconduct, Egbert’s framework requires leaving any further damages remedy in this domain to Congress, not the courts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Although Egbert v. Boule instructs that Bivens expansion is disfavored and that courts should decline a new implied remedy whenever there is even one rational reason to think Congress is better positioned to act, that analysis presupposes the meaningful availability of an “alternative remedial structure.” Here, the alleged facts describe not merely an Eighth Amendment excessive-force episode but deliberate officer obstruction of the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program (28 C.F.R. § 542.10 et seq.), which undermines the very “alternative” Egbert relies upon and leaves a practical remedial void. Recognizing a narrowly cabined damages action for egregious, purposeless force coupled with intentional foreclosure of administrative relief aligns with Carlson v. Green’s recognition of a Bivens remedy for Eighth Amendment violations and serves the constitutional interest in basic procedural fairness and deterrence where executive processes are intentionally made unavailable. Limiting the remedy to this rare circumstance also mitigates Ziglar v. Abbasi’s separation-of-powers concerns by avoiding broad judicial management of prisons while still providing accountability when officers themselves defeat the prescribed channels.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether courts may extend the implied Bivens damages remedy to an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officials when the alleged abuse was egregious and officers allegedly obstructed the Bureau of Prisons’ administrative remedies.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Eighth Amendment (cruel and unusual punishment) as enforced via an implied damages action under Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents; with collateral relevance of the Bureau of Prisons’ administrative remedy program (ARP) and the Prison Litigation Reform Act’s exhaustion framework (as background special-factor/alternative-remedy considerations).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue the Fourth Circuit improperly created a new Bivens cause of action for prisoner excessive-force claims—a context the Supreme Court has repeatedly warned courts not to expand into (especially after Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert v. Boule). They contend Congress and the Executive have already provided alternative mechanisms for prisoner complaints (e.g., the BOP grievance system and other processes), and that recognizing personal-capacity damages actions will chill prison officials and intrude into prison administration. The United States as amicus supports petitioners and frames the question broadly: Bivens should not be extended to Eighth Amendment excessive-force claims in prisons.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues the decision below is a deliberately narrow, fact-bound application of the post-Egbert framework to a “rare” scenario: ‘rogue’ frontline officers allegedly committed extreme physical abuse with no penological justification and then intentionally prevented access to the very administrative remedies that would otherwise count as alternative remedial structures. On that framing, the Fourth Circuit did not authorize a general Bivens remedy for all prisoner excessive-force claims; it recognized (at most) a narrow extension only when officials both commit egregious abuse and affirmatively thwart the available remedial scheme, leaving no meaningful alternative remedy. Respondent also maintains petitioners attack an overbroad version of the holding (‘catastrophic consequences’) that other courts have already treated as limited to its unusual facts.
key_precedents: Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)
Booker v. S.C. Dep’t of Corr., 855 F.3d 533 (4th Cir. 2017)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the most serious point: if officers themselves sabotaged the ARP, treating it as an “alternative remedial structure” risks insulating unconstitutional force. But Egbert’s instruction is categorical in the relevant respect—the question is whether Congress/the Executive has created a remedial framework and whether there is any rational reason to think the political branches should decide on damages, not whether the framework functioned in this case; obstruction may bear on PLRA exhaustion under Ross v. Blake, but Ross does not supply authority to imply a new cause of action. Carlson does not resolve the extension question because, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, excessive force by line officers is a meaningfully different context from medical indifference, and Abbasi/Egbert treat even modest differences as triggering hesitation given prison-administration and systemic-litigation concerns. I would reverse on narrow grounds: this is a new context and the PLRA/ARP are sufficient alternative remedial structures to foreclose a Bivens extension, leaving any tailored remedy for sabotage-and-force claims to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that officers’ alleged obstruction of the ARP makes the “alternative remedial structure” illusory, but Egbert v. Boule makes clear that the relevant question is whether Congress or the Executive has provided a remedial scheme at all—not whether it worked perfectly in a given case—and that courts may not create a new damages action to cure perceived gaps. Carlson v. Green does not supply a general Eighth Amendment damages remedy; an excessive-force claim is a meaningfully different context from Carlson’s medical-indifference setting, and under Ziglar v. Abbasi that difference triggers the presumption against extension. Ross v. Blake, invoked by Justice Sotomayor, concerns PLRA exhaustion and “availability” of administrative remedies; it does not authorize courts to imply a cause of action absent text or congressional enactment. On an originalist and separation-of-powers view, any expansion of personal-capacity damages for federal prisoners is for Congress, and uncertainty itself is a reason to stop under Egbert.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that officers allegedly obstructed the ARP, so the “alternative remedial structure” is illusory in practice, and she invokes Ross v. Blake to emphasize unavailability. But under Egbert, the relevant question is not whether the alternative process worked in this plaintiff’s case; it is whether Congress or the Executive has provided a remedial structure such that courts have reason to leave any additional damages remedy to the political branches. Ross speaks to PLRA exhaustion and when administrative remedies are “available,” not to whether Article III courts may create a new implied damages action. Even accepting the egregious facts, extending Carlson to excessive-force/obstruction claims would still be a new context with separation-of-powers and prison-administration consequences that Abbasi and Egbert instruct us not to undertake.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts is right to stress Egbert’s instruction that the mere existence of an alternative remedial scheme can be a reason to hesitate, even if it fails in a particular case, and Justice Kagan similarly argues Ross v. Blake is “only” about PLRA exhaustion. But when the alleged constitutional wrong includes officers’ deliberate sabotage of the very administrative channel the Court is told to treat as the alternative, that is not simply “imperfect operation” of a scheme—it is state-created unavailability that makes the asserted substitute non-remedial in any meaningful sense, which bears directly on whether an “alternative remedial structure” actually counsels hesitation. Nor do I accept that this is meaningfully outside Carlson: an Eighth Amendment claim by a federal prisoner against line officers for individualized, contrary-to-policy abuse is the same core setting of prison-custody constitutional injury, and Abbasi/Egbert’s systemic-policy fears are not triggered by recognizing damages for rogue brutality. Under my pragmatic approach, denying any damages remedy here risks insulating the most grievous misconduct against the most vulnerable, eroding deterrence and access to justice where Congress has not clearly foreclosed Carlson’s already-recognized Eighth Amendment foothold.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point that officer obstruction makes the ARP “illusory” is forceful as a matter of fairness, and Justice Jackson’s refinement—that sabotage by the same officers undermines the premise of an “alternative”—sharpens the concern. But as the Chief Justice notes, Egbert frames the inquiry at the level of institutional design: whether Congress/the Executive have created a remedial structure such that courts have rational reason to leave damages to the political branches, not whether it was thwarted in this plaintiff’s case. Ross v. Blake (which Sotomayor and Jackson invoke) affects my analysis only to the extent it shows obstruction can excuse PLRA exhaustion; it does not supply authority to recognize a new implied cause of action where Abbasi/Egbert treat even Carlson-adjacent extensions—like excessive force versus medical indifference—as “new contexts” triggering hesitation. On my pragmatic textualist view, the administrability and separation-of-powers costs of case-by-case “unavailability” as a Bivens trigger are exactly the kind of judicial calibration Egbert says we should not undertake.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness point—that officers’ obstruction makes the ARP illusory and thus demands a Carlson-style damages remedy—is powerful as a matter of equity, but it does not overcome Egbert’s separation-of-powers rule that the existence of a remedial framework is itself a rational reason to leave damages design to Congress. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Ross v. Blake speaks to when exhaustion is excused because remedies are “unavailable”; it cannot be transmuted into affirmative authority for Article III courts to create a new implied cause of action. Nor does Carlson control, because—under Abbasi’s “new context” inquiry—an excessive-force claim against line officers differs in kind from medical-indifference and carries distinct risks of judicial supervision over prison discipline and use-of-force decisions. If officers sabotaged the ARP, the answer is to enforce existing rules (including excusing exhaustion where appropriate) and to leave any further damages remedy to Congress, not to extend Bivens.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the most serious point: if officers can obstruct the ARP, treating that scheme as an “alternative remedial structure” risks leaving grave Eighth Amendment abuse without accountability. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Egbert instructs that the existence of a congressionally/administratively created remedial framework itself supplies a rational reason to leave any incremental damages remedy to Congress, even if the framework is thwarted in a particular case. Ross v. Blake, which Justice Sotomayor invokes, concerns when PLRA exhaustion is excused because remedies are “unavailable”; it does not authorize Article III courts to create a new implied cause of action, and obstruction may bear on exhaustion but not on extending Bivens. Carlson’s medical-indifference context remains meaningfully different from an excessive-force claim against line officers, and under Abbasi/Egbert that difference—coupled with prison-administration and systemic-litigation consequences—requires judicial restraint.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s most forceful point is that officer obstruction renders the ARP practically unavailable and risks insulating egregious Eighth Amendment misconduct, and Justice Jackson similarly argues that sabotage defeats Egbert’s premise of meaningful alternatives. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Egbert frames the inquiry at the level of institutional design: the existence of a congressionally/administratively created remedial scheme (including the PLRA’s choices) supplies a rational reason for courts to refrain, even if the scheme fails in a particular case. Ross v. Blake, as Justice Kagan notes, is about excusing PLRA exhaustion when remedies are “unavailable,” not about authorizing an implied damages action where Congress has not provided one. Carlson does not control because an excessive-force claim against line officers presents a meaningfully different context with prison-administration and systemic-litigation implications that Abbasi and Egbert treat as special factors counseling hesitation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is that Egbert treats the existence of an alternative remedial structure as a sufficient “rational reason” to hesitate, without case-by-case inquiry into whether it worked here. But where (as pleaded) the very officers accused of Eighth Amendment violence also deliberately make the ARP functionally unavailable, the supposed alternative is not merely imperfect—it is defeated by government actors in a way that undercuts Egbert’s premise that the political branches have supplied a meaningful substitute for judicial enforcement. Justice Kagan is right that Ross v. Blake is an exhaustion case, yet Ross’s unavailability principle is still relevant to the “special factors” analysis because it shows the danger of treating a sabotaged procedure as an adequate accountability mechanism when deciding whether damages are necessary to deter constitutional abuse. On these narrow allegations—frontline, gratuitous force plus intentional obstruction of the only internal remedy—I do not view this as recalibrating prison policy so much as preserving Carlson’s core accountability logic in an adjacent Eighth Amendment setting.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert v. Boule, recognizing a damages remedy beyond the three established Bivens contexts is a "disfavored judicial activity," and an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officials presents a new context distinct from Carlson v. Green’s medical-indifference claim. Egbert further instructs that the existence of an alternative remedial structure—here the Bureau of Prisons’ administrative remedy program, together with Congress’s detailed treatment of prison litigation in the PLRA—counsels hesitation, and courts may not extend Bivens simply because the remedial scheme may be ineffective or unavailable in a particular case. Allegations that officers obstructed grievances may bear on PLRA exhaustion (i.e., whether remedies were “available”), but they do not authorize the Judiciary to create a new implied cause of action that Congress has not provided. Respect for separation of powers, federalism, and institutional legitimacy therefore requires reversing and leaving any expansion of prisoner-damages remedies to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: An implied damages action is not found in the text of the Eighth Amendment, and this Court has repeatedly held that extending Bivens beyond its narrow, historically recognized settings is a “disfavored judicial activity.” Egbert v. Boule and Ziglar v. Abbasi require courts to reject any new Bivens context whenever there is even a rational reason to think Congress—not the Judiciary—should decide whether to authorize damages, and prison administration and officer discipline present quintessential separation-of-powers and federalism concerns. The existence of alternative remedial structures, including the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and Congress’s comprehensive regulation of prisoner litigation through the PLRA, counsels against judicially creating a new cause of action even if those mechanisms are imperfect or allegedly obstructed. Whatever the egregiousness of the alleged conduct, recognizing a new Eighth Amendment excessive-force Bivens remedy would expand Carlson v. Green into a meaningfully different context that Egbert and Hernandez v. Mesa forbid.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Egbert v. Boule and Ziglar v. Abbasi, extending Bivens is now a "disfavored" judicial activity, and the presence of even one "special factor"—including any alternative remedial structure—requires courts to refrain from creating a damages remedy. Federal prisoners have alternative mechanisms, including the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and the availability of injunctive relief, and Egbert makes clear that courts may not add a damages remedy simply because existing remedies are incomplete or allegedly ineffective in a given case. Recognizing a new Eighth Amendment excessive-force Bivens action in the prison setting would intrude into prison administration and risk chilling necessary force decisions, a separation-of-powers concern that counsels hesitation. Carlson does not control because this is a new context (excessive force and grievance obstruction rather than deliberate indifference to medical needs), and post-Abbasi/Egbert the Court has repeatedly refused to extend Bivens beyond its narrow historical confines.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: This case involves alleged, gratuitous Eighth Amendment abuse by frontline federal prison officers coupled with affirmative obstruction of the Bureau of Prisons’ administrative remedy program, which undercuts the government’s claim that an “alternative remedial structure” meaningfully exists in practice. While Egbert v. Boule and Ziglar v. Abbasi caution against expanding Bivens, Carlson v. Green already recognizes an Eighth Amendment Bivens remedy for federal prisoners, and an excessive-force claim against individual officers acting contrary to prison policy is not meaningfully different in a way that triggers systemic, policy-making concerns. Where officers themselves render the ARP unavailable, the PLRA’s exhaustion framework (as explained in Ross v. Blake) confirms that formal remedies cannot be treated as adequate substitutes, and fairness and deterrence require a damages remedy for egregious constitutional abuse. Denying any remedy in these circumstances would leave the most vulnerable—incarcerated people subject to violence by their keepers—without realistic access to justice and would weaken enforcement of the Eighth Amendment’s core prohibition.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert v. Boule, extending Bivens is a “disfavored” judicial activity, and an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against line-level federal prison officers presents a new context beyond the three recognized settings (including Carlson’s medical-care claim). Egbert instructs that if Congress or the Executive has created an alternative remedial structure—here, the BOP’s Administrative Remedy Program against the backdrop of the PLRA—courts may not “second-guess that calibration” by superimposing a damages remedy, even if the process is allegedly thwarted in a particular case. The alleged obstruction is serious, but the workability and separation-of-powers concerns Abbasi and Egbert emphasize—judicial intrusion into prison administration and Congress’s choice not to authorize personal-capacity damages for these claims—counsel leaving any gap-filling to Congress. On that framework, the Fourth Circuit’s fact-bound approach still amounts to an extension, and Egbert directs that uncertainty itself is a reason to stop.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: This claim seeks to extend Bivens into a new context—an Eighth Amendment excessive-force suit against federal prison officials—distinct from the settings in Bivens, Davis, and even Carlson, and under Ziglar v. Abbasi a new context triggers a strong presumption against judicially implied damages remedies. Under Egbert v. Boule, courts may not create a new Bivens action if there is any rational reason to think Congress is better suited to decide, and the existence of alternative remedial structures (including the BOP’s administrative remedy program and Congress’s comprehensive prison-litigation scheme in the PLRA) supplies at least one such reason even if those mechanisms are imperfect or allegedly obstructed. Allowing damages claims here would invite federal-court intrusion into prison administration and supervision of line officers—precisely the separation-of-powers concern Abbasi and Egbert instruct courts to avoid. The proper course is to leave any expansion of prisoner remedies against federal officials to Congress, not to judicial implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: This claim arises in a new Bivens context because the Court has recognized implied damages remedies only in three settings, and an Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim against federal prison officers is meaningfully different from Carlson’s Eighth Amendment medical-indifference context. Under Egbert v. Boule and Ziglar v. Abbasi, a court may not extend Bivens if there is any rational reason to think Congress is better positioned to decide whether to authorize damages, and the existence of the Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and the PLRA’s detailed exhaustion framework are alternative remedial structures counseling hesitation even if a plaintiff alleges they were obstructed. Recognizing this remedy would intrude into prison administration and carry systemwide litigation and deterrence consequences—precisely the kind of special-factors concern that Egbert and Hernandez instruct courts to leave to the political branches. The proper course is judicial restraint: adhere to precedent while declining to create a new implied cause of action beyond Bivens, Carlson, and Davis.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Egbert v. Boule, the two-step Bivens inquiry largely collapses to whether there is any reason to think Congress is better equipped to create a damages remedy, and even a single rational reason to pause forecloses extension. An Eighth Amendment excessive-force claim by a federal prisoner presents a new context beyond the three recognized Bivens settings (including Carlson’s medical-indifference context), and recognizing a new personal-capacity remedy would intrude into prison administration and raise separation-of-powers concerns emphasized in Ziglar v. Abbasi. The Bureau of Prisons’ Administrative Remedy Program and Congress’s detailed regulation of prisoner litigation through the PLRA—including its exhaustion framework—constitute alternative remedial structures that counsel hesitation even if an officer allegedly obstructed them, because the existence of a remedial scheme is itself a reason to leave remedial design to Congress rather than courts. Precedent thus requires declining to imply a new damages action here notwithstanding the alleged egregious facts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Egbert v. Boule instructs courts not to extend Bivens when there is any rational reason to think Congress is better positioned to provide a remedy, including where the political branches have created an alternative process. But this case’s alleged facts—that frontline officers committed gratuitous Eighth Amendment violence and then intentionally blocked the Bureau of Prisons’ ARP—implicate procedural fairness and leave the existing “alternative remedial scheme” functionally unavailable, undermining the deterrence rationale recognized in Carlson v. Green for Eighth Amendment harms in federal custody. Treating this as a narrow, fact-bound extension avoids opening a general prison-administration damages regime (Abbasi; Egbert) while ensuring there is some meaningful accountability when officers themselves sabotage the only designed remedial channel. In these circumstances, allowing the claim to proceed best vindicates the Eighth Amendment’s protection against cruel and unusual punishment without second-guessing the branches’ calibration so much as addressing its alleged obstruction.
